en.title: Master of Laws (LL.M): the whole course
en.short: What an LL.M is, how it is organised, the main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text:
These notes are for learning. They are not legal advice and cannot tell you what to do about a real case or transaction. If you have a legal problem, speak to a qualified lawyer in the relevant country.

Law changes. Statutes are amended and repealed, treaties are revised, and courts overrule earlier decisions. Check the current official text before relying on any rule here.

Every rule belongs to a country or a treaty regime, and these notes say which. A rule of Nigerian law does not apply in Kenya, and an English decision does not bind a court in Ghana or Nigeria.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
The Master of Laws, usually written LL.M or LLM, is a postgraduate degree in law. It is not a first law degree. Most students already hold a Bachelor of Laws (LLB) or a Juris Doctor (JD). Some programmes admit graduates of other fields, who take foundation courses first.

An LL.M is usually specialised. You take a cluster of advanced subjects, such as international law, commercial and financial law, or human rights, and you write a dissertation.

In most countries the LL.M does not by itself qualify you to practise. In Nigeria you still need the Nigerian Law School programme and call to the Bar. In England and Wales, solicitors now qualify through the Solicitors Qualifying Examination and barristers through the Bar course. Check your own regulator.

sections.heading: How the programme is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and award differ by country and institution. Check your own student handbook for the rules that bind you.

Common patterns:
Nigeria: a university postgraduate degree, often one to two years full-time, with coursework and a dissertation. University programmes are regulated by the National Universities Commission.
England and Wales: a taught LL.M commonly runs one year full-time or two years part-time, with taught modules and a dissertation.
Some universities offer an LL.M by research, examined by thesis alone.

Most programmes use a credit system. Modules are examined by coursework, written examination or both. The dissertation is supervised and examined, sometimes with an oral defence, called a viva.

Part-time and distance study are common, especially for working lawyers.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Foundations. Advanced Legal Research and Dissertation Design teaches you to find, manage and cite sources. Comparative Legal Method teaches you to compare two systems without confusing them. Advanced Jurisprudence and Legal Reasoning, with Rule of Law and Constitutionalism, supplies the theory.

Public international law. Advanced Public International Law covers sources, subjects, state responsibility and dispute settlement. Advanced Human Rights Law, International Humanitarian Law and International Criminal Law build on it.

Economic and commercial law. International Trade Law, International Investment Law, International Commercial Arbitration, Corporate Governance, Competition Law, Intellectual Property Law, Tax Law and Policy, Banking and Financial Regulation, and Insolvency and Restructuring Law.

Law, resources and society. Environmental Law and Climate Change, Energy and Natural Resources Law, Gender, Law and Society, Law and Development in Africa, Legal Pluralism and Customary Law, and Transitional Justice.

Practice and justice. Advanced Criminal Justice and Penal Policy, Advanced Evidence and Proof, and Legal Ethics and Professional Regulation.

The LL.M Dissertation draws the programme together.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Work from primary sources. Read the statute, treaty, regulation or judgment itself. Textbooks and journal articles explain the law; they are not the law.

For every authority, record the jurisdiction, the date, the exact provision or paragraph, and whether it is still in force. Keep this in one research file. Use an official gazette or a citator to check that a statute has not been repealed and a case not overruled.

Read one good journal article per topic and note its argument, not only its conclusion. Master’s work is judged on analysis, not description. Start the dissertation early: choose a narrow question, review the literature, and agree the method with your supervisor.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Citing law that is no longer in force, or a case that has been overruled.

Assuming one country’s rule is universal. Name the jurisdiction every time.

Treating a blog post, Wikipedia or a lecture slide as authority.

Confusing binding with persuasive authority. A foreign decision is persuasive at most, unless a local court has adopted it.

Describing a case or statute without stating the principle it establishes.

Ignoring the handbook’s word limit, citation style and deadline, or leaving the dissertation to the last months.

keyPoints: An LL.M is a postgraduate law degree for graduates; it is not a first law degree.
In most countries an LL.M does not by itself qualify you to practise law.
Every rule belongs to a country or a treaty regime, so name it every time.
Read primary sources and check that they are still in force.
Master’s assessment rewards analysis and argument, not description.
Start the dissertation early and agree the method with your supervisor.

en.title: Advanced Legal Research and Dissertation Design
en.short: Framing research questions, choosing methods, finding and updating sources, citation, plagiarism and proposals.

sections.heading: Research question
sections.text: Begin with a topic, then turn it into a research question: a clear, answerable question naming the legal issue, jurisdiction and time frame. 'Is Nigeria’s justice system efficient?' is too broad. Amina, a student in Nigeria, narrows it to: 'In one named High Court, did the civil procedure rules introduced in a stated year reduce the time from filing to first hearing in contract cases?' The question now points to sources and methods. Check that your dissertation can answer it with available time and data.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Doctrinal method analyses legal rules from legislation, cases and official materials, tracing how a rule developed and how courts apply it. Comparative method compares two or more legal systems, but you must justify why they are comparable and avoid assuming a rule can be transplanted. Empirical method collects evidence: case-file data, interviews, surveys or statistics. It needs a sample, ethics approval and care with consent and anonymity. Theoretical method uses concepts from jurisprudence or social theory to explain or critique the law. The method must fit the question; many dissertations combine two.

sections.heading: Sources and updating
sections.text: Primary sources are the law itself: constitutions, statutes, regulations, cases, treaties and official gazettes. Secondary sources explain it: textbooks, journal articles, digests and law reform reports. Use official or reliable databases and record the date you accessed online material. Law changes, so update by checking amendments, repeals and later cases. Tools that trace later cases, and official gazettes, help, but availability varies. State the research date and verify the current text before submission.

sections.heading: Citation and proposal
sections.text: Cite every legal proposition and every borrowed idea. Follow your institution’s style, such as OSCOLA or Bluebook, or its local guide. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words or ideas as your own; quote and cite directly, and do not copy your own earlier work without permission. A dissertation proposal should state the title, background, question, literature review, method, sources, chapter outline, timetable, ethics and expected contribution. Get supervisor approval before writing.

keyPoints: A research question must name the legal issue, jurisdiction and time frame, and be answerable with available sources.
Doctrinal method analyses rules from legislation and cases; comparative method compares systems only when comparability is justified.
Empirical method uses case files, interviews, surveys or statistics and requires ethics approval and a clear sample.
Primary sources are legislation, cases, treaties and gazettes; secondary sources explain them, and both must be updated to the research date.
Cite every legal proposition and borrowed idea in your institution’s style; plagiarism includes using another’s words or ideas without credit.
A proposal should set out the question, literature, method, sources, chapter plan, timetable, ethics and expected contribution.

en.title: Comparative Legal Method
en.short: Purposes and limits of comparison, functionalist and cultural methods, choosing jurisdictions and translating concepts.

sections.heading: Why compare
sections.text: Comparative legal method is the systematic study of two or more legal systems to understand, explain or improve law. It serves law reform, harmonisation, teaching and judicial reasoning. Its limits matter. A comparison can be selective, and rules may look alike while working differently. Law is tied to language, history, institutions and culture. The researcher must state the purpose, jurisdictions and sources, and check current official texts because law changes.

sections.heading: Two approaches
sections.text: The functionalist approach asks what problem a rule solves and compares rules that perform the same function. It is useful for law reform but can assume that all systems face the same problems. The cultural approach treats law as part of social life and asks how people understand and use it. It guards against false similarities but can overstate difference. Good work combines both: compare functions, then test the comparison against context.

sections.heading: Choosing and translating
sections.text: Choose jurisdictions for a reason: a shared legal family (systems with common history and method), similar economy, historical connection, reliable sources, or a contrasting solution. A Nigerian study might use the UK for common law, the US for federalism, South Africa for its mixed system, and France for civil law. Translating concepts is hard. 'Consideration', the common law requirement of exchange, is not the French 'cause' (the reason for an obligation, replaced by a 'lawful and certain content' rule in France’s 2016 contract reform). A trust has no exact French equivalent; the fiducie is a limited statutory cousin. Use functional equivalence, keep the original term, and explain it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A researcher asks whether French law has a trust. The English trust separates legal title from beneficial ownership. French law has no identical institution. A functionalist compares the trust with the fiducie and with company and security devices. A cultural approach explains the different history of property and notarial practice. The careful conclusion is that the fiducie is a partial functional equivalent, not the same thing. The same caution applies to customary law in Nigeria and South Africa: compare it as living law, not as a single code.

keyPoints: Comparative legal method compares two or more systems to understand, reform or harmonise law.
Functionalism compares rules by the problem they solve; the cultural approach stresses context and meaning.
Choose jurisdictions for stated reasons such as shared legal family, similar economy or contrasting solution.
Translation requires functional equivalence, not word-for-word matching.
English 'consideration' is not French 'cause', which France reformed in 2016, and a trust has no exact French equivalent.
Always check current official sources and do not present one country’s law as universal.

en.title: Advanced Jurisprudence and Legal Reasoning
en.short: Positivism, natural law, realism, critical theory, precedent, discretion and a case example; not legal advice.

sections.heading: Positivism and natural law
sections.text: Legal positivism holds that law exists by social sources, not by moral merit. Hart’s rule of recognition identifies valid rules in a legal system; Austin treated law as commands. Natural law ties legal validity or obligation to practical reason and morality. Fuller argued that law must satisfy an inner morality, including publicity and prospectivity. Finnis grounds law in basic goods, such as life and knowledge. The debate is whether unjust rules are law: positivists may call them law but morally bad; natural lawyers often say they are not fully law. These are general theories, applied differently in each legal system.

sections.heading: Realism and critique
sections.text: Legal realism, especially American realism, doubts that rules alone decide cases. It studies what officials do and predicts court behaviour. Critical legal studies argue that legal reasoning often masks political choices. Feminist and critical race theories examine how law can reproduce gender and racial inequality. These schools differ, so treat them as families of argument, not one doctrine.

sections.heading: Rules and precedent
sections.text: Rules apply all-or-nothing; principles have weight and may conflict. Dworkin used principles to argue that judges should interpret law as integrity, deciding cases so the law forms one coherent scheme of principle. In common law systems such as England and Wales, Nigeria and Ghana, precedent binds: the ratio decidendi, the reason for the decision, is authoritative; obiter dicta, remarks not necessary to the decision, are persuasive. Courts distinguish cases on facts or overrule earlier decisions. Civil law systems such as France treat precedent differently.

sections.heading: Discretion and case
sections.text: Hart’s open texture means general rules have borderline cases where judges exercise discretion. Dworkin’s law as integrity resists this, though critics dispute whether it yields one right answer. In Riggs v Palmer (1889, New York, United States), a statute appeared to let a murderer inherit under a will. The court refused, using the principle that no one may profit from wrongdoing. The case shows reasoning with principles, precedent and discretion. Check current statutes and cases; this is study material, not legal advice.

keyPoints: Legal positivism identifies law by social sources; natural law links legal validity or obligation to morality.
Legal realism studies what courts and officials do; critical theories examine how law can mask or reproduce power.
Rules apply all-or-nothing, while principles have weight and can conflict.
In common law systems, the ratio decidendi binds and obiter dicta are persuasive only.
Hart’s open texture supports judicial discretion in hard cases; Dworkin’s law as integrity resists it.
In Riggs v Palmer (1889, New York), a principle defeated a literal statute, showing theory in legal reasoning.

en.title: Rule of Law and Constitutionalism
en.short: Competing rule-of-law theories, constitutionalism, judicial review, emergencies and compliance measures.

sections.heading: Competing meanings
sections.text: The rule of law is contested. A thin version, associated with Joseph Raz, requires law to be clear, prospective, stable and applied by independent courts; it says little about law’s content. Dicey’s English account stressed equality before the law. A thick version adds substantive justice and human dignity. No definition is neutral.

sections.heading: Constitutionalism and courts
sections.text: Constitutionalism means limiting government by law, not merely having a constitution. It usually combines separation of powers, checks and balances, and judicial review. In the US, Marbury v Madison (1803) established that courts may strike down unconstitutional legislation. The UK has no codified constitution; parliamentary sovereignty means courts cannot invalidate Acts of Parliament, though they review administrative legality. Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution declares itself supreme in section 1, and courts can void inconsistent laws. South Africa’s 1996 Constitution, section 1(c), makes the rule of law a founding value; the Constitutional Court may review legislation.

sections.heading: Emergency powers
sections.text: Emergencies test constitutionalism. Governments claim extra powers to restore order, but these can become permanent or abusive. Safeguards include legislative approval, time limits, judicial review and non-derogable rights. South Africa’s section 37 allows a state of emergency only under an Act of Parliament, with parliamentary approval and court control. The UK’s Civil Contingencies Act 2004 permits temporary emergency regulations, subject to parliamentary scrutiny. Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution, section 305, sets conditions for a state of emergency. The US Constitution allows suspension of habeas corpus only in limited cases. Exceptions can swallow the rule.

sections.heading: Measuring compliance
sections.text: Measuring compliance is difficult. Formal indicators count constitutional text, independent courts and legal certainty. Substantive indicators ask whether people, especially the poor, can use law to challenge power. The World Justice Project Rule of Law Index ranks countries using surveys and expert questionnaires, but it measures perceptions and its method is debated. Rankings can reward stability while missing injustice. Compare several sources and check the current edition, because scores change yearly.

keyPoints: Thin theories of the rule of law stress formal qualities of law; thick theories add substantive justice and human dignity.
Constitutionalism limits government through law, separation of powers and judicial review.
Marbury v Madison (1803) established judicial review in the US; the UK relies on parliamentary sovereignty and administrative review.
Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution is supreme under section 1; South Africa’s 1996 Constitution makes the rule of law a founding value in section 1(c).
Emergency powers need legislative approval, time limits, judicial control and respect for non-derogable rights.
Rule-of-law indices such as the World Justice Project Index measure perceptions and should be read with other sources.

en.title: Advanced Public International Law
en.short: Sources, treaties, statehood, jurisdiction, immunities, use of force, state responsibility and reform debates.
keywords: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties

sections.heading: Sources and treaties
sections.text:
Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute lists treaties, customary international law and general principles as sources, with judicial decisions and writings as subsidiary means. Custom needs widespread and consistent state practice accepted as law (opinio juris).

The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 governs the making, interpretation, reservations and ending of treaties between states. A party cannot invoke internal law to justify breach under Article 27. Reservations are barred if prohibited or contrary to the treaty’s object and purpose.

sections.heading: Statehood and jurisdiction
sections.text:
Statehood under the Montevideo Convention 1933, article 1, requires a permanent population, defined territory, government and capacity to enter relations. Declaratory theory says recognition acknowledges statehood; constitutive theory says it creates statehood.

Jurisdiction is a state’s power to prescribe and enforce. Prescriptive grounds include territoriality, nationality, protective principle and universal jurisdiction. Enforcement is generally territorial. Immunities limit jurisdiction: the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961 protects diplomats, and state immunity protects states in foreign courts, subject to debated exceptions.

sections.heading: Force and responsibility
sections.text:
UN Charter Article 2(4) prohibits the threat or use of force. Exceptions are self-defence under Article 51 and Security Council action under Chapter VII. In Nicaragua v United States (1986), the ICJ found the United States responsible for supporting the contras and for breaches of the use of force and non-intervention rules.

State responsibility arises from an internationally wrongful act: conduct attributable to the state and a breach of an international obligation, under the ILC Articles 2001. Consequences include cessation and reparation.

sections.heading: Municipal law and reform
sections.text:
Monism treats international and municipal law as one system; dualism treats them as separate, so treaties need domestic enactment. In Nigeria, section 12 of the 1999 Constitution requires treaty enactment by the National Assembly.

The African Union’s Constitutive Act 2000, article 4(h), allows intervention in a member state for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity on an Assembly decision. Reform debates include Security Council expansion and the veto, limits on self-defence, cyber operations, and state immunity and human rights claims.

keyPoints: Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute lists treaties, custom, general principles and subsidiary sources.
The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 governs treaties, and internal law cannot justify breach.
Montevideo criteria guide statehood, while declaratory and constitutive theories disagree on recognition.
Jurisdiction rests on territoriality, nationality, protective principle and universal grounds, and immunities limit it.
UN Charter Article 2(4) bans force, except self-defence under Article 51 and Chapter VII action.
State responsibility needs attribution and breach; AU Constitutive Act article 4(h) permits intervention in grave cases.

en.title: Advanced Human Rights Law
en.short: UN, African, European and Inter-American human rights systems, limitations, ESC rights and business duties.

sections.heading: Global system
sections.text:
The UN system rests on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights 1948 and the two 1966 Covenants: the ICCPR for civil and political rights and the ICESCR for economic, social and cultural rights. The Human Rights Council reviews states and receives complaints; treaty bodies monitor implementation.

The ICCPR allows limits only if prescribed by law and necessary to protect others or public order, for example article 19(3) on expression. Article 4 permits derogation in a public emergency threatening the life of the nation, but not for non-derogable rights such as freedom from torture.

sections.heading: Regional systems
sections.text:
The African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights 1981 protects civil, political, economic, social, cultural and peoples’ rights. The African Commission examines state reports and communications; the African Court hears direct individual cases only against states that have made a special declaration accepting individual applications.

The European Convention on Human Rights 1950 is enforced by the European Court of Human Rights, which hears individual applications against Council of Europe states. The American Convention on Human Rights 1969 uses the Inter-American Commission and Court. Each system has its own admissibility rules; check current texts.

sections.heading: ESC rights and business
sections.text:
Economic, social and cultural rights include health, housing, education and work. Under ICESCR article 2(1), states realise them progressively to the maximum of available resources, while non-discrimination and some core duties are immediate.

The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights 2011 set three pillars: the state duty to protect, corporate responsibility to respect, and access to remedy. They are soft law, not a treaty.

sections.heading: Enforcement example
sections.text: Suppose Amina, a Nigerian journalist, is detained for a report. She may complain to the UN Human Rights Committee if Nigeria accepts the ICCPR petition procedure, and to the African Commission. A European parallel would go to the European Court after domestic remedies. Remedies vary; regional decisions may need domestic implementation.

keyPoints: The UDHR 1948 and the two 1966 Covenants are the core UN instruments.
ICCPR limits must be lawful and necessary; article 4 derogations cannot touch non-derogable rights.
The African Charter protects civil, political, economic, social, cultural and peoples’ rights and is monitored by the African Commission.
The European system is enforced by a court; the Inter-American system uses a commission and a court, with different access rules.
ICESCR rights are realised progressively, but non-discrimination is immediate.
The UN Guiding Principles are soft law based on protect, respect and remedy.

en.title: International Humanitarian Law
en.short: Classification, combatants, civilians, conduct of hostilities, war crimes, Geneva law and enforcement.

sections.heading: Conflict classification
sections.text: International humanitarian law (IHL), or the law of armed conflict, applies once armed conflict exists. An international armed conflict (IAC) is armed force between states. A non-international armed conflict (NIAC) is protracted armed violence between a state and an organised armed group, or between such groups, with intensity and organisation. Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions 1949 applies to NIACs; Additional Protocol II 1977 applies above a higher threshold. IACs are governed by the four Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol I.

sections.heading: Combatants and civilians
sections.text: In an IAC, combatants are members of a party’s armed forces, apart from medical and religious personnel. They may be targeted and, if captured, are entitled to prisoner-of-war status. In a NIAC, IHL binds fighters but gives no same combatant privilege; domestic law may prosecute them. Civilians are all persons who are not combatants. In doubt, a person is presumed civilian. Civilians lose protection from direct attack only while directly participating in hostilities.

sections.heading: Conduct of hostilities
sections.text: The cardinal rules are distinction, proportionality and precautions. Distinction requires parties to attack only military objectives and never to make civilians or civilian objects the object of attack. Proportionality forbids an attack expected to cause incidental civilian harm excessive to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Precautions require constant care, verification of targets, choice of means and methods, and warning where circumstances permit. An attack that becomes excessive must be cancelled or suspended.

sections.heading: War crimes and enforcement
sections.text: War crimes are serious violations of IHL punishable individually. Grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and Protocol I apply in IACs; serious violations of Common Article 3 and Protocol II may be war crimes in NIACs. Rome Statute Article 8 lists war crimes. Enforcement rests on Common Article 1, ICRC action, state responsibility and criminal prosecution, including universal jurisdiction for grave breaches. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the ICC convicted Thomas Lubanga Dyilo in 2012 for enlisting and using children under 15 in hostilities in Ituri, a NIAC.

keyPoints: IHL applies in IACs and NIACs; Common Article 3 covers NIACs and Additional Protocol II applies above a higher threshold.
In IACs, combatants may be targeted and get prisoner-of-war status; civilians are all non-combatants and are presumed civilian in doubt.
Distinction limits attacks to military objectives; proportionality forbids excessive incidental civilian harm; precautions require verification and warnings.
War crimes are serious IHL violations punishable individually; grave breaches apply in IACs and serious Common Article 3 or Protocol II violations may be war crimes in NIACs.
Common Article 1 requires states to respect and ensure respect; enforcement includes ICRC action, state responsibility and criminal prosecution.
The ICC convicted Thomas Lubanga Dyilo in 2012 for enlisting and using children under 15 in hostilities in Ituri, DRC, a NIAC.

en.title: International Criminal Law
en.short: Core crimes, liability, ICC and hybrid tribunals, complementarity, immunities and African cases.

sections.heading: Core crimes
sections.text:
International criminal law punishes individuals for the most serious crimes. Genocide, article 6 of the Rome Statute, requires acts done with intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Crimes against humanity, article 7, require a widespread or systematic attack on a civilian population.

War crimes, article 8, are serious violations of the laws of armed conflict. Aggression, article 8 bis, covers planning, preparation, initiation or execution of an act of aggression by a person in a position effectively to control or direct a state’s political or military action, which by its character, gravity and scale manifestly violates the UN Charter.

sections.heading: Liability and courts
sections.text:
Modes of liability decide who is responsible. Article 25(3) covers committing, ordering, soliciting, aiding and abetting, and contributing to a common purpose. Article 28 makes commanders responsible for failing to prevent or punish crimes by forces under their effective control.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) is permanent. The Yugoslavia and Rwanda tribunals were created by the UN Security Council. Hybrid courts, like the Special Court for Sierra Leone, mix international and national law. In 2012 the ICC convicted Lubanga for enlisting and conscripting children under 15 and using them in hostilities in DRC.

sections.heading: Complementarity and immunities
sections.text:
The ICC is complementary to national courts. Under article 17, a case is inadmissible if a state with jurisdiction is genuinely investigating or prosecuting it, unless the state is unwilling or unable.

Article 27 says official capacity, including head of state, does not bar ICC jurisdiction. Before national courts, incumbent heads of state and foreign ministers may still enjoy immunity, as the ICJ held in the Arrest Warrant case (DRC v Belgium, 2002).

sections.heading: African cases
sections.text:
African states have referred cases to the ICC, including Uganda, the DRC and the Central African Republic. The court has tried Lubanga, Katanga, Bemba and Ongwen. It has issued warrants for Omar al-Bashir, then President of Sudan.

The African Union has criticised the ICC for focusing on Africa and has debated collective withdrawal. Supporters reply that African states referred many cases and that complementarity puts the duty to prosecute first at home.

keyPoints: Genocide requires intent to destroy a protected group; crimes against humanity require a widespread or systematic attack on civilians.
War crimes are serious violations of the laws of armed conflict; aggression concerns manifest violations of the UN Charter.
Article 25(3) of the Rome Statute sets out modes of liability, and article 28 covers command responsibility.
The ICC is complementary: national courts have the first duty to investigate and prosecute.
Article 27 removes official capacity as a bar before the ICC, but national immunity rules can still apply.
African states have referred cases to the ICC, and the African Union has criticised its focus on Africa.

en.title: International Trade Law
en.short: WTO rules on goods, services and IP, dispute settlement, regional trade agreements, AfCFTA and development.

sections.heading: WTO framework
sections.text: The WTO, established in 1995 by the Marrakesh Agreement, administers GATT 1994 for goods, GATS for services and TRIPS for intellectual property. Most-favoured-nation (MFN) treatment requires an advantage given to one member to be given to all, subject to exceptions. National treatment requires imports, once inside the border, to be treated no less favourably than like domestic goods, services or rights. Members bind maximum tariffs in schedules and must publish trade rules. Exceptions cover health, security, customs unions and free trade areas.

sections.heading: Dispute settlement
sections.text: The WTO Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU) governs disputes. A member complains; consultations follow; a panel rules; the Dispute Settlement Body adopts the report unless all members reject it. The Appellate Body hears appeals on law. Since December 2019 it has lacked a quorum because the United States blocked appointments. Some members use the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA). Check the current position.

sections.heading: Regional agreements and AfCFTA
sections.text: GATT Article XXIV and GATS Article V allow regional trade agreements (RTAs) that meet coverage conditions and do not raise barriers to outsiders. They are exceptions to MFN. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) was signed in Kigali on 21 March 2018 and entered into force on 30 May 2019. It aims to liberalise goods and services. Suppose Ada in Nigeria makes shirts for a Ghanaian buyer. Ghana applies the AfCFTA tariff only if the shirts meet the rules of origin (the tests that decide which country a product counts as coming from) and have proof of origin; otherwise the normal tariff applies. Check current schedules.

sections.heading: Trade and development
sections.text: GATT Part IV calls for better market access for developing countries. The 1979 Enabling Clause permits developed members to give differential and more favourable treatment, including tariff preferences for developing-country goods under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP). WTO agreements contain special and differential treatment (SDT), such as longer transition periods for developing and least-developed countries (LDCs). The Doha Development Agenda, launched in 2001, stalled. The Cotton Four (Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad and Mali) pressed cotton subsidies. The effect of SDT is debated.

keyPoints: The WTO administers GATT for goods, GATS for services and TRIPS for intellectual property.
MFN and national treatment are core non-discrimination rules, subject to exceptions.
The DSU provides panel and appellate review, but the Appellate Body has lacked a quorum since December 2019.
GATT Article XXIV and GATS Article V permit RTAs as exceptions to MFN.
The AfCFTA, in force since 30 May 2019, aims to liberalise African trade subject to rules of origin and current schedules.
Special and differential treatment and the Enabling Clause give developing countries flexibility, though their effect is debated.

en.title: International Investment Law
en.short: Treaty protections, expropriation, FET, ICSID arbitration, reform debates and African responses.

sections.heading: Treaties and standards
sections.text: An international investment agreement is a treaty between states protecting investors of one state who invest in the other. Most are bilateral investment treaties (BITs). Core standards are national treatment, most-favoured-nation treatment, fair and equitable treatment (FET), full protection and security, free transfer of funds and protection from expropriation. The Salini test (Salini v Morocco, 2001) helps define what counts as an investment.

sections.heading: Expropriation and FET
sections.text:
Expropriation is direct when title is taken, indirect when a measure has equivalent effect (Metalclad v Mexico, 2000). It is lawful only for a public purpose, without discrimination, with due process and with compensation, usually fair market value. The Hull formula (prompt, adequate, effective) frames the compensation debate.

FET is the claim most often argued. Tribunals read it to cover arbitrariness, denial of justice and frustrated legitimate expectations. An umbrella clause turns a contractual promise into a treaty duty; SGS v Pakistan (2003) read it narrowly, SGS v Philippines (2004) broadly.

sections.heading: Arbitration
sections.text: Treaties usually let an investor arbitrate against the state; consent is given in the treaty, though some require local proceedings or a waiting period first. The main forum is ICSID, created by the 1965 Washington Convention. Others use UNCITRAL, ICC or LCIA rules. An ICSID award binds the parties and is enforced in member states like a final judgment. There is no appeal; annulment lies under Article 52 on limited grounds. Other awards are enforced under the New York Convention 1958.

sections.heading: Sovereignty and reform
sections.text: Critics say investor-state dispute settlement lets investors bypass domestic courts and chills regulation. Defenders say it depoliticises disputes and lowers risk. UNCITRAL Working Group III has discussed reform since 2017, including a code of conduct and an appeal mechanism. South Africa terminated several BITs and enacted the Protection of Investment Act 22 of 2015, which puts domestic law and local remedies first. The Morocco-Nigeria BIT, signed in 2016, adds investor duties; check whether it is in force.

keyPoints: Investment treaties protect foreign investors through standards such as national treatment, MFN, FET and protection from expropriation.
Lawful expropriation needs a public purpose, non-discrimination, due process and compensation.
FET is the most litigated standard and covers arbitrariness and frustrated legitimate expectations.
ICSID arbitration is created by the 1965 Washington Convention; annulment is limited to Article 52 grounds.
South Africa’s Protection of Investment Act 2015 puts domestic law and local remedies first.
Reform debates concern bypass of domestic courts, regulatory chill and a possible appeal mechanism.

en.title: International Commercial Arbitration
en.short: Arbitration agreements, tribunal powers, applicable law, awards, setting aside, and New York Convention enforcement.

sections.heading: Agreement and tribunal
sections.text:
An arbitration agreement submits disputes to arbitrators rather than courts. It may be a contract clause or a separate agreement. Separability means the clause survives the main contract’s invalidity. Competence-competence lets the tribunal rule on its own jurisdiction. Parties choose the number of arbitrators, often one or three, and their appointment. Rules or a court may appoint if a party fails. Tribunals can order interim measures and set procedure, subject to the seat’s law and fair hearing.

Example: a Lagos buyer and a Nairobi seller arbitrate in London under LCIA Rules. If the sale contract is invalid, the tribunal may still hear the dispute because the clause is separate, unless the clause itself is invalid.

sections.heading: Law and institutions
sections.text: The seat is the legal place of arbitration. Its law, the lex arbitri, governs procedure and the supervisory court. Parties choose the substantive law for the merits; without choice, the tribunal applies conflict rules. Institutional rules supply procedure, such as ICC, LCIA and SIAC rules. The UNCITRAL Rules are for ad hoc arbitration, that is, arbitration without an administering institution. Institutions appoint tribunals, decide challenges and fix costs.

sections.heading: Awards and setting aside
sections.text: An award is the tribunal’s decision. A party may ask the court at the seat to set it aside. The grounds include incapacity, invalid agreement, lack of notice, excess of scope, irregular procedure, non-arbitrability and public policy. England’s Arbitration Act 1996 allows challenge for substantive jurisdiction, serious irregularity, and, unless excluded, error of law. Nigeria’s Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023, based on the UNCITRAL Model Law, provides similar grounds. Setting aside is not an appeal on the merits.

sections.heading: Recognition and enforcement
sections.text: The New York Convention 1958 requires Contracting States to recognise and enforce foreign arbitral awards. Article III sets the general duty. Article IV lists documents to supply. Article V allows refusal on limited grounds, such as invalid agreement, lack of notice, excess of scope, irregular procedure, non-arbitrability, public policy, or setting aside at the seat. Reservations, including reciprocity, are possible. Check the current status and text. Enforcement is before a competent court.

keyPoints: An arbitration agreement may be a clause or a separate contract, and separability keeps it alive if the main contract fails.
Competence-competence allows the tribunal to decide its own jurisdiction.
The seat’s law, the lex arbitri, governs procedure and the supervisory court, while parties choose the substantive law.
Awards are final and can be set aside only on limited grounds at the seat, not by a full appeal on the merits.
The New York Convention 1958 requires Contracting States to enforce foreign awards, subject to limited refusal grounds in Article V.
Institutional rules such as ICC, LCIA and SIAC, and the UNCITRAL Rules for ad hoc arbitration, provide procedure and appointment mechanisms.

en.title: Corporate Governance
en.short: Agency problems, directors’ duties, shareholder rights, takeovers and codes in the UK, Nigeria and South Africa.

sections.heading: Agency and accountability
sections.text: Corporate governance is the system of rules and practices by which companies are directed and controlled. An agency problem arises when shareholders (the principals) delegate management to directors (the agents), whose interests may differ. Monitoring, bonding and residual loss (value lost to the conflict) are agency costs. Boards answer through independent directors, audit committees and disclosure. Example: in Lagos, Chief Ade’s company gives a supply contract to a firm owned by his brother without tender. Minority shareholders object. Good governance requires disclosure of the conflict and approval by disinterested directors.

sections.heading: Duties and rights
sections.text: Directors owe duties to the company, not usually to individual shareholders. UK Companies Act 2006 sections 171 to 177 codify duties: act within powers, promote the success of the company for members as a whole, exercise independent judgment, use reasonable care, skill and diligence, avoid conflicts, not accept benefits and declare interests. Section 172 also requires regard to employees, suppliers, customers, community and environment. Nigeria’s Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 (CAMA) regulates directors and shareholder remedies; check its sections. Shareholders normally vote, receive accounts, appoint and remove directors, and sue for wrongs done to themselves; wrongs to the company are usually claimed by the company itself, though shareholders may bring derivative claims in limited cases. Disclosure of material and related-party information makes these rights real.

sections.heading: Takeovers and stakeholders
sections.text: Takeover regulation protects shareholders when control changes. Common rules are equal treatment, a mandatory bid after a control threshold, no frustrating action without shareholder approval, and disclosure. The UK Takeover Code and Companies Act 2006 Part 28 apply. South Africa’s Companies Act 71 of 2008 Chapter 5 and Takeover Regulations apply. Nigeria regulates takeovers mainly through the Investments and Securities Act and SEC rules; check the current text. Shareholder primacy says directors should maximise shareholder value. Stakeholder theory says consider employees, creditors and communities. UK section 172 adopts enlightened shareholder value. Codes include the UK Corporate Governance Code (comply or explain), the Nigerian Code of Corporate Governance 2018 (mandatory for listed and other covered companies) and South Africa’s King IV (apply and explain).

keyPoints: An agency problem arises when ownership is separated from control and managers’ interests diverge from shareholders'.
Directors owe duties to the company; UK Companies Act 2006 sections 171 to 177 codify them.
Shareholder rights depend on voting, information, appointment and removal powers, and litigation.
Takeover rules commonly require equal treatment, disclosure and a mandatory bid after a control threshold.
The UK Code uses comply or explain; South Africa’s King IV uses apply and explain; Nigeria’s 2018 Code is mandatory for listed and other covered companies.
Shareholder primacy and stakeholder theory disagree on whose interests directors should serve.

en.title: Competition Law
en.short: Goals, cartels, abuse of dominance, merger control, economics and enforcement in the EU, US, Nigeria and South Africa.

sections.heading: Goals and framework
sections.text: Competition law aims to protect competition and consumer welfare, and sometimes wider public interest. Goals are contested: some stress efficiency, others fairness. It prohibits cartels, abuse of dominance and anticompetitive mergers. The main legal sources differ by country: EU Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union articles 101 and 102 and Merger Regulation 139/2004; US Sherman Act 1890 and Clayton Act 1914; Nigeria’s Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018; South Africa’s Competition Act 89 of 1998. Check the current text.

sections.heading: Conduct and mergers
sections.text: A cartel is an agreement among competitors to fix prices, share markets or rig bids. Abuse of dominance is conduct by a dominant firm that forecloses rivals or exploits buyers. Merger control reviews mergers before completion. In the EU, the Commission assesses whether a merger significantly impedes effective competition. South Africa’s Act also allows public interest factors, such as employment and ownership by historically disadvantaged persons.

sections.heading: Economics and enforcement
sections.text: Economic analysis defines the market and measures market power. Market definition asks which products and areas constrain the firm. The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) sums squared market shares. If shares are 40, 30, 20 and 10 per cent, HHI = 1600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3000. If the 30 and 20 firms merge, shares become 40, 50, 10, so HHI = 1600 + 2500 + 100 = 4200, a rise of 1200. Enforcement is by public agencies, such as the European Commission, US Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice, Nigeria’s FCCPC and South Africa’s Competition Commission. Remedies include fines, leniency for cartel members who confess and cooperate, behavioural orders, divestiture and private damages.

keyPoints: Competition law protects competition and consumer welfare, and sometimes public interest.
Cartels are agreements among competitors to fix prices, share markets or rig bids.
Abuse of dominance concerns conduct by a dominant firm that harms rivals or buyers.
Merger control reviews mergers before completion; South Africa’s Act includes public interest factors.
The HHI sums squared market shares; a merger raising it from 3000 to 4200 adds 1200 points.
Enforcement uses fines, leniency, behavioural orders, divestiture and private damages.

en.title: Intellectual Property Law
en.short: Copyright, patents, trademarks, trade secrets, plant varieties, treaties and African IP debates.

sections.heading: Copyright and patents
sections.text: Copyright protects original literary, artistic, musical and dramatic works, and often software, for a limited term. It arises automatically; no registration is needed in Berne countries. Patents protect inventions that are new, involve an inventive step and are capable of industrial application. A patent gives a limited monopoly in exchange for disclosure. In Nigeria, the Copyright Act 2022 governs copyright; the Patents and Designs Act (Cap P2, Laws of the Federation 2004) governs patents. Ghana has the Copyright Act 2005 (Act 690) and Patents Act 2003 (Act 654). Terms and formalities differ by country, so check the current statute.

sections.heading: Marks, secrets, varieties
sections.text: Trademarks protect signs that distinguish goods or services and can last indefinitely if renewed. Trade secrets protect confidential commercial information, such as formulas or customer lists, where secrecy is maintained. Plant variety rights protect new plant varieties; they are separate from patents. Nigeria’s Plant Variety Protection Act 2021 and Kenya’s Seeds and Plant Varieties Act (Cap 326) are examples. The UPOV Convention sets international standards, but not all African states are members. Each right has different scope, exceptions and remedies.

sections.heading: Treaties and African debates
sections.text: The Berne Convention 1886 sets copyright minimum standards. The Paris Convention 1883 covers industrial property. The WTO TRIPS Agreement 1994 requires members to protect IP but allows flexibilities. The Doha Declaration 2001 confirms that TRIPS should not prevent access to medicines. A compulsory licence lets a government authorise use without the owner’s consent, usually with payment. African debates include compulsory licensing and local production of medicines, as in South Africa’s Competition Commission investigations into antiretroviral pricing, which ended in settlements allowing generic licences. Traditional knowledge, such as medicinal plants and designs, is often misappropriated. ARIPO’s Swakopmund Protocol 2010 and OAPI’s Bangui Agreement address some forms. Critics say conventional IP can ignore communal ownership and farmers’ rights; others stress incentives for innovation. Check current national law and treaty membership.

keyPoints: Copyright protects original expression and usually arises automatically; patents protect new, inventive and useful inventions; many countries examine applications, though Nigeria mainly registers them without full examination.
Trademarks identify goods or services; trade secrets protect confidential commercial information.
Plant variety rights are a separate system from ordinary patents.
Berne, Paris and TRIPS set minimum international standards; TRIPS contains flexibilities.
The Doha Declaration 2001 says TRIPS should not block access to medicines.
African debates concern compulsory licensing, local production, traditional knowledge and farmers’ rights; check current law.

en.title: Tax Law and Policy
en.short: Income, corporate and VAT tax, residence, treaties, transfer pricing, avoidance and development.

sections.heading: Core taxes
sections.text:
Income tax charges persons on income; corporate tax charges companies on profits; value added tax (VAT) is an indirect tax on consumption, borne by buyers. Taxable income is assessable income minus allowable deductions. VAT payable is output VAT minus input VAT. Rates vary by country and year.

Example: net sales 1,000,000, allowable expenses 600,000, profit 400,000. At an assumed 30% corporate rate, tax is 120,000. Output VAT 75,000 minus input VAT 45,000 gives VAT payable 30,000. The 7.5% VAT rate is illustrative.

sections.heading: Residence and treaties
sections.text:
Residence decides whether a country taxes worldwide income; source decides whether it taxes income arising in its territory. Individuals are often resident where they have a permanent home or habitual abode; companies where incorporated or centrally managed. Tests vary.

Nigeria taxes residents on worldwide income and non-residents on Nigerian-source income. The UK uses residence rules, with special rules for foreign income. South Africa taxes residents on worldwide income and non-residents on South African-source income. Double taxation arises when two states tax the same income. Treaties, based on OECD or UN models, give relief by credit or exemption. Transfer pricing requires related companies to price cross-border transactions at arm’s length, as unrelated parties would.

sections.heading: Administration and development
sections.text:
Tax administration covers registration, filing, assessment, collection and appeals. Nigeria’s Federal Inland Revenue Service (renamed the Nigeria Revenue Service from 2026), the UK’s HM Revenue and Customs and the South African Revenue Service are the main authorities. Tax avoidance is arranging affairs to reduce tax within the law; tax evasion is illegal, such as hiding income. Countries use general anti-avoidance rules (GAARs), for example the UK GAAR in Finance Act 2013 and South Africa’s GAAR in sections 80A to 80L of the Income Tax Act 58 of 1962. Nigeria has relied on specific provisions and judicial doctrines; a statutory GAAR takes effect under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 from 2026.

Tax funds public services. Base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS) is tax planning that shifts multinational profits to low-tax places. The OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework has agreed a 15% global minimum tax for large multinationals, but implementation varies. Tax policy must balance revenue, fairness and growth.

keyPoints: Income tax is on persons, corporate tax on company profits, and VAT on consumption.
Taxable income = assessable income − allowable deductions; VAT payable = output VAT − input VAT; tax = taxable profit × rate.
Residence and source decide which country may tax; treaties relieve double taxation by credit or exemption.
Transfer pricing applies the arm’s length principle to related-party cross-border transactions.
Tax avoidance is legal planning; evasion is illegal; GAARs and specific rules counter avoidance.
Tax policy affects development through revenue, incentives and BEPS; rates and rules vary by country and year, so check current law.

en.title: Banking and Financial Regulation
en.short: Bank supervision, capital, deposit insurance, resolution, central banking, payments, fintech, AML and stability.

sections.heading: Supervision
sections.text: Banking regulation sets entry, conduct and safety rules; supervision checks compliance. Prudential rules concern solvency and liquidity; conduct rules concern fair customer treatment. Licensing and supervision usually sit with a central bank or dedicated agency. Examples: the Central Bank of Nigeria under the CBN Act 2007; the Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority in the United Kingdom, created by the Financial Services Act 2012 under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 framework; the Central Bank of Kenya under its banking law. Details differ by country; check the current statute and rulebook.

sections.heading: Capital and safety nets
sections.text:
Capital adequacy requires loss-absorbing capital against risk-weighted assets (RWA). Basel III sets minimum common equity Tier 1 of 4.5 per cent, Tier 1 of 6 per cent and total capital of 8 per cent, plus buffers; national rules may be stricter. Example: CET1 capital 5 and RWA 100 give 5 ÷ 100 = 5 per cent. That meets 4.5 per cent but is below 7 per cent with a 2.5 per cent conservation buffer.

Deposit insurance repays insured depositors on failure; Nigeria’s NDIC and the UK’s FSCS are examples, and limits change. Resolution seeks orderly failure, using bail-in (imposing losses on a bank’s creditors) and other tools. Examples: the UK Banking Act 2009, EU Directive 2014/59/EU, and Nigeria’s AMCON Act 2010 (a bad-bank vehicle created in response to the 2009 crisis).

sections.heading: Central banking and payments
sections.text: Central banks conduct monetary policy, lend in crisis and oversee payments. Settlement finality (a completed payment cannot be reversed) and real-time gross settlement reduce risk. Examples: the CBN, Bank of England and European Central Bank. Mobile systems such as M-Pesa in Kenya need licensing and consumer safeguards.

sections.heading: Fintech, AML and stability
sections.text: Fintech rules cover e-money, digital lending and crypto assets; sandboxes allow controlled testing. Anti-money laundering law follows the FATF (Financial Action Task Force) Recommendations: customer due diligence, records and suspicious transaction reports. Examples: Nigeria’s Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022, UK Money Laundering Regulations 2017 and Kenya’s Proceeds of Crime and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2009. Stability lessons include the 2007-09 global crisis, Nigeria’s 2009 banking crisis and Ghana’s 2017-2019 cleanup.

keyPoints: Prudential supervision protects solvency and liquidity; conduct supervision protects customers.
Basel III minimums are 4.5 per cent common equity Tier 1, 6 per cent Tier 1 and 8 per cent total capital, plus buffers.
CET1 ratio = CET1 capital ÷ risk-weighted assets.
Deposit insurance and resolution protect depositors and allow orderly bank failure.
Central banks oversee payment systems and act as lender of last resort.
AML rules require customer due diligence and suspicious transaction reports.

en.title: Insolvency and Restructuring Law
en.short: Liquidation, administration, receivership, creditor priorities, security and cross-border insolvency.

sections.heading: Forms and aims
sections.text: Insolvency law deals with a debtor that cannot pay its debts. Liquidation, or winding up, ends the company: assets are sold and proceeds distributed. Administration is a rescue process in which an administrator runs the company under court protection while a plan is prepared. Receivership is appointment by a secured creditor to enforce security over assets. Restructuring changes debts or operations to keep the business alive, through a scheme of arrangement, a company voluntary arrangement or business rescue. The UK uses the Insolvency Act 1986, the Enterprise Act 2002 and the Corporate Insolvency and Governance Act 2020. Nigeria’s main company insolvency statute is the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020. South Africa’s Companies Act 71 of 2008 provides business rescue. Check the current text.

sections.heading: Priorities and security
sections.text: Security gives a creditor rights over assets if the debtor defaults. A fixed charge covers an identified asset; a floating charge covers changing assets. On insolvency, a secured creditor is usually paid from its security first, but process costs and preferential claims (debts the law puts first, such as some wages and taxes) may rank ahead. Unsecured creditors share what remains. Example: Ada Foods Ltd owes Bank A 30 million secured by a fixed charge over its factory, and owes suppliers 20 million unsecured. The factory sells for 50 million. Ignoring costs, Bank A receives 30 million, leaving 20 million for the estate; preferential claims may take from that, and the rest goes to unsecured creditors. Check local priority rules.

sections.heading: Cross-border cases
sections.text: Cross-border insolvency arises when a debtor has assets or creditors in more than one country. The UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency 1997 helps courts recognise foreign proceedings, give representatives access, grant relief and cooperate. It distinguishes main proceedings, at the debtor’s centre of main interests (COMI), from non-main proceedings where the debtor has an establishment. South Africa adopted the Model Law by Cross-Border Insolvency Act 42 of 2000. The UK adopted it through Cross-Border Insolvency Regulations 2006. Nigeria has not adopted the Model Law; its courts rely on statute and common law, so check current position.

keyPoints: Liquidation ends the company; administration and business rescue aim to rescue it.
Receivership enforces a secured creditor’s rights over charged assets.
Secured creditors usually rank ahead of unsecured creditors, subject to expenses and preferential claims.
The UNCITRAL Model Law supports recognition, access and cooperation in cross-border insolvency.
South Africa adopted the Model Law by Act 42 of 2000; the UK by Regulations 2006; Nigeria has not adopted it.
Always check the current statute and local priority rules.

en.title: Environmental Law and Climate Change
en.short: Environmental principles, EIA and liability, UNFCCC and Paris law, carbon markets and just transition.

sections.heading: Principles and regulation
sections.text:
Environmental law governs use of air, water, land and living things. Its core principles include prevention, precaution (lack of full proof is not a reason to delay cost-effective action), polluter pays, sustainable development and public participation.

Regulation usually mixes command-and-control rules, such as permits and emission standards, with economic instruments such as charges. Check the current national statute and regulations. In Nigeria, NESREA (National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency) enforces environmental standards.

sections.heading: Liability and EIA
sections.text:
Environmental liability may be civil, criminal or administrative. It can rest on fault or, for some activities, on strict liability (no fault need be proved); remedies include clean-up orders, fines and damages.

Environmental impact assessment (EIA) is a procedure before approval: screening, scoping, study, public participation and a decision. It does not itself grant permission. In South Africa, section 28 of the National Environmental Management Act 1998 imposes a duty of care and remediation. Nigeria’s EIA Act 1992 requires assessment for projects likely to have significant effects on the environment.

sections.heading: Climate treaty law
sections.text:
The UNFCCC 1992 is the framework treaty. The Kyoto Protocol 1997 set quantified emission targets for listed developed countries. The Paris Agreement 2015 applies to all parties: each submits a nationally determined contribution (NDC) and updates it; the aim is to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C. Paris also has transparency rules and Article 6 on cooperative approaches.

African states negotiate through the African Group of Negotiators. Nigeria’s Climate Change Act 2021 and Kenya’s Climate Change Act 2016 create domestic frameworks.

sections.heading: Carbon markets and transition
sections.text:
Carbon markets put a price on emissions. Cap-and-trade sets a total limit and lets firms trade allowances; baseline-and-credit systems reward cuts below a baseline. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allows internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) and a central mechanism. Rules must prevent double counting and ensure additionality (cuts beyond business as usual).

Just transition means sharing the costs of moving to a low-carbon economy fairly, especially for workers and communities. The Paris preamble mentions just transition and decent work. African priorities stress adaptation finance and energy access.

keyPoints: Environmental law uses principles such as prevention, precaution, polluter pays and public participation, but rules vary by country.
EIA is a pre-decision process; it does not itself authorise a project.
Liability can be civil, criminal or administrative, and may be strict for some activities.
The UNFCCC is the framework; Kyoto set targets for listed developed countries; Paris applies to all parties through NDCs.
Article 6 allows carbon market cooperation, but rules must prevent double counting and ensure additionality.
Just transition addresses fair sharing of costs, and African states emphasise adaptation finance and energy access.

en.title: Energy and Natural Resources Law
en.short: Ownership, licensing, host agreements, decommissioning, local content and transition in Nigeria, Ghana and South Africa.

sections.heading: Ownership and licensing
sections.text:
Countries treat petroleum, minerals and electricity differently. In Nigeria, the Petroleum Industry Act 2021 regulates petroleum licences and leases and created regulators and the national oil company, while the Minerals and Mining Act 2007 covers solid minerals. Ghana’s Minerals and Mining Act 2006 (Act 703) and Petroleum (Exploration and Production) Act 2016 (Act 919) govern mineral and petroleum rights. South Africa’s Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act 28 of 2002 makes mineral and petroleum resources a common heritage, with the State, acting through the Minister, as custodian.

Electricity is licensed separately: Nigeria’s Electricity Act 2023, Ghana’s Energy Commission Act 1997 (Act 541) for licensing and the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission Act 1997 (Act 538) for tariffs and service, and South Africa’s Electricity Regulation Act 4 of 2006, with NERSA as regulator under the National Energy Regulator Act 2004. These notes are for learning, not legal advice. Check the current text, because these laws change.

sections.heading: Contracts and stabilisation
sections.text:
Host government agreements (HGAs) allocate risk between state and investor. Common forms are concessions, production sharing contracts and service contracts. A stabilisation clause tries to protect the investor from later law or tax changes. It may freeze the law, require renegotiation, or give compensation. Such clauses are controversial: they can limit a state’s right to regulate for the environment or public health.

Example: an investor signs a petroleum agreement with Ghana at an agreed royalty rate. If Ghana later raises the rate, a stabilisation clause may require renegotiation or compensation. The outcome depends on the clause and the applicable law.

sections.heading: Decommissioning, local content and transition
sections.text:
Decommissioning is the safe removal or abandonment of wells, platforms and pipelines at the end of a project. Laws increasingly require plans and financial security. Local content rules require operators to buy local goods and employ local workers. Nigeria’s local content law, the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development Act 2010, and Ghana’s Petroleum (Local Content and Local Participation) Regulations 2013 (L.I. 2204) are examples.

The energy transition shifts investment from fossil fuels to renewables. It raises stranded asset risk (assets that lose value before the end of their planned life), grid and licensing questions, and just transition concerns for workers and communities. South Africa’s renewable energy procurement programme is one response. Students should compare how each country balances investor protection, state control and climate duties.

keyPoints: Petroleum and minerals are owned or held in trust by the state in Nigeria, Ghana and South Africa, but the legal form differs.
Licensing separates upstream petroleum (exploration and production), mining and electricity, and each country has its own regulator.
Host government agreements allocate risk; stabilisation clauses may freeze law, require renegotiation or provide compensation.
Decommissioning rules require end-of-life plans and financial security.
Local content laws require local goods, services and workers, for example Nigeria’s 2010 Act and Ghana’s L.I. 2204.
Energy transition law must balance climate goals, stranded assets and just transition.

en.title: Gender, Law and Society
en.short: Equality, CEDAW and Maputo rights, violence, family and customary law, and women’s economic life in Africa.

sections.heading: Equality and CEDAW
sections.text: Equality means treating like cases alike, but substantive equality asks whether rules and structures disadvantage women in practice. Direct discrimination is different treatment on grounds such as sex; indirect discrimination is a neutral rule that harms one sex more. The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), 1979, defines discrimination in article 1 and obliges states in article 2 to end it. Article 4 permits temporary special measures. The Maputo Protocol, adopted in 2003, repeats these duties for African states in article 2.

sections.heading: Violence and Family
sections.text: Gender-based violence is discrimination because it denies women equal enjoyment of rights. CEDAW’s text does not name violence, but Committee General Recommendations 19 and 35 do. Maputo Protocol article 4 expressly requires states to prevent and punish violence. Domestic violence statutes include Nigeria’s Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015, Ghana’s Domestic Violence Act 2007 and Kenya’s Protection Against Domestic Violence Act 2015. Family law falls under CEDAW article 16 and Maputo articles 6, 7 and 21, covering marriage, divorce and inheritance.

sections.heading: Customary Law Debates
sections.text: Many African states recognise customary law alongside statute and common law. Customary rules on marriage and inheritance may discriminate, but many constitutions make customary law subject to equality guarantees. In South Africa, Bhe v Magistrate, Khayelitsha (2005) struck down male primogeniture in customary inheritance as unconstitutional. Debates divide between reforming customary law from within, using the idea of living customary law, and abolishing rules that deny women equal rights. The choice is political and cultural as well as legal.

sections.heading: Economic Life
sections.text: Economic life includes paid work, land, credit, inheritance and unpaid care. CEDAW article 11 requires equal employment opportunities and article 13 covers economic and social benefits. Maputo Protocol article 13 adds economic and social welfare rights. In practice, customary inheritance and land rules often limit women’s security. Kenya’s Matrimonial Property Act 2013 recognises contributions to marriage property, including non-monetary work. Debates ask whether formal rights change household bargaining or need enforcement, legal aid and social support.

keyPoints: Substantive equality goes beyond identical treatment and asks whether rules disadvantage women in practice.
CEDAW article 1 defines discrimination against women and article 2 obliges states to eliminate it.
The Maputo Protocol gives African states specific treaty duties on violence, marriage and economic rights.
Gender-based violence is treated as discrimination under CEDAW Committee recommendations and Maputo Protocol article 4.
Customary law is usually subject to constitutional equality, as Bhe v Magistrate, Khayelitsha (2005) shows in South Africa.
Economic rights depend on enforcement, legal aid and reform of inheritance and land rules.

en.title: Law and Development in Africa: Legacies, Institutions and Resources
en.short: Colonial legal legacies, rule of law, land, resources, courts and informal justice in African development.

sections.heading: Colonial legacies
sections.text: Colonial administrations left layered legal systems. British indirect rule preserved customary authorities in colonies such as Nigeria and Ghana, while French assimilation pressed a unitary civil-law model in Senegal. Legal pluralism means state law, customary law, religious law and informal norms coexist. It can give accessible rules, but it can also create uncertainty and unequal protection, especially for women and outsiders.

sections.heading: Rule of law
sections.text: The rule of law means law is public, predictable and applied equally, with independent courts. Development is broader than GDP growth: it includes capabilities, security and participation. Scholars disagree about causation. Some argue inclusive legal institutions encourage investment and growth; others warn that legal transplants (laws borrowed from other countries) fail when they ignore local context. A practical test is whether a small firm can enforce a contract without political influence.

sections.heading: Land and resources
sections.text: Land law shapes development: land is collateral, shelter and identity. In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in each state governor in trust for all Nigerians and converts existing rights into rights of occupancy: statutory rights of occupancy for urban land and customary rights of occupancy for non-urban land. Customary tenure holds land collectively and is not always written down; registration can secure or displace it. Natural resources raise the resource curse: mineral wealth can fund development, but weak institutions invite corruption and conflict. The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), East African Community (EAC) and Southern African Development Community (SADC) coordinate trade and infrastructure. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) aims to liberalise trade across Africa.

sections.heading: Courts and informal justice
sections.text: Courts can check executive power, protect rights and make rules predictable. Access is limited by cost, delay, distance and language. Informal justice through chiefs, elders, customary courts and religious bodies is often nearer and cheaper. It can also reflect local power and discriminate. South Africa’s Constitution, section 211(3), requires courts to apply customary law when it applies, subject to the Constitution and legislation dealing with customary law. Regional courts, such as the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, add another layer. Ghana, Kenya and South Africa show different outcomes under similar rules.

keyPoints: Colonial rule left legal pluralism, with state, customary, religious and informal norms coexisting in many African countries.
The rule of law supports development through predictability and independent courts, but causation is contested and legal transplants often fail when they ignore local context.
Land law affects development; Nigeria’s Land Use Act 1978 vests land in state governors in trust for all Nigerians and converts rights to rights of occupancy.
Natural resource wealth can fund development, but weak institutions may invite corruption and conflict, often called the resource curse.
Regional integration through ECOWAS, EAC, SADC and AfCFTA aims to expand trade and infrastructure.
Courts and informal justice both resolve disputes; informal systems are accessible but can discriminate, so constitutional safeguards matter.

en.title: Legal Pluralism and Customary Law
en.short: How state, customary, religious and informal justice systems coexist in Africa, with rights debates.

sections.heading: Plural legal orders
sections.text: Legal pluralism means more than one legal order governs the same people or place. State courts apply statutes and common law; customary law derives from a community’s customs; religious law, such as Islamic law, governs personal matters for believers; informal justice includes elders, chiefs and community mediation. These systems overlap and compete. A person may use a state court for land and a family council for marriage. The state claims final authority, but its reach is uneven.

sections.heading: Recognition and accommodation
sections.text: Constitutions accommodate pluralism differently. Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution recognises customary courts and Sharia Courts of Appeal in states that establish them. Ghana’s 1992 Constitution makes customary law part of the common law (article 11). Kenya’s 2010 Constitution permits traditional dispute resolution only if it respects the Bill of Rights and does not conflict with the Constitution or written law (article 159(2)(c) and (3)), and establishes Kadhi courts for Muslim personal law (article 170). South Africa’s 1996 Constitution requires courts to apply customary law when applicable, subject to the Constitution and specific legislation (section 211(3)).

sections.heading: Codification and choice of law
sections.text: Codification writes customary rules into statutes or restatements, making them certain but potentially rigid. Choice of law rules decide which system applies: personal law, subject matter, place or agreement. Nigeria’s internal conflict rules may ask whether parties are subject to customary law and whether a custom is repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience. South Africa’s Recognition of Customary Marriages Act 120 of 1998 codifies some marriage rules.

sections.heading: Rights debates
sections.text: Customary and religious systems can offer accessible justice and cultural legitimacy. Critics reply that they may entrench gender inequality or deny fair hearing. In Bhe v Magistrate, Khayelitsha (2005), South Africa’s Constitutional Court struck down male primogeniture in customary inheritance as unconstitutional. In Ukeje v Ukeje (2014), Nigeria’s Supreme Court held that customary law denying female children inheritance was discriminatory. Courts are reshaping custom through constitutional rights. The debate is how to protect equality without destroying legitimate cultural practice. Rules differ by country and change, so check current law.

keyPoints: Legal pluralism is the coexistence of state, customary, religious and informal justice systems in one social field.
Constitutions recognise customary law but usually subject it to constitutional rights, statute and specific legislation.
Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa accommodate pluralism through different constitutional and statutory rules.
Choice of law rules and codification decide which norm applies and can make customary law more certain but less flexible.
Courts have struck down discriminatory customary rules, as in Bhe v Magistrate, Khayelitsha (South Africa, 2005) and Ukeje v Ukeje (Nigeria, 2014).
Check the current constitution, statute and case law because pluralism rules differ by country and change over time.

en.title: Transitional Justice
en.short: Accountability, truth commissions, reparations, amnesty and reform in South Africa, Rwanda and Sierra Leone.

sections.heading: Core measures
sections.text: Transitional justice is the set of judicial and non-judicial measures a society uses after conflict or repression to address widespread abuses. Its main measures are accountability through prosecutions, truth commissions that record patterns and hear victims, reparations such as compensation or memorials, amnesty, and institutional reform such as vetting officials (screening out those linked to abuses) and reforming courts and police. These measures can support each other, but they also trade off. Prosecutions may deter, yet they can disturb a fragile peace. Amnesty may secure a settlement, but blanket amnesty can deny victims a remedy. Reparations may be material or symbolic. Reform aims to prevent repetition.

sections.heading: African cases
sections.text: South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, created by the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act 34 of 1995, traded conditional amnesty for full disclosure and heard both victims and perpetrators. Rwanda used the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, set up by UN Security Council Resolution 955 in 1994, for senior leaders, and community gacaca courts (local lay panels based on traditional dispute resolution) for many genocide cases. Sierra Leone used the Special Court for Sierra Leone, established in 2002, for those bearing greatest responsibility, alongside a Truth and Reconciliation Commission under its 2000 Act. Charles Taylor was convicted by the Special Court in 2012. These cases show different mixes of courts, truth-seeking and local participation.

sections.heading: Peace and law
sections.text: Transitional justice links to international criminal law when domestic courts cannot or will not act, and to peacebuilding when it seeks to rebuild trust and institutions. International law limits amnesty for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, though state practice varies. The choice between peace and justice is often presented as a dilemma, but the measures can be sequenced. Students should check the current treaty text, Security Council resolutions and national statutes, because rules and institutions change.

keyPoints: Transitional justice combines prosecutions, truth commissions, reparations, amnesty and institutional reform after mass abuse.
Accountability seeks to end impunity, but it may conflict with peace settlements.
Truth commissions record patterns of abuse and give victims a voice; they are not usually criminal courts.
Reparations can be material or symbolic; amnesty can be conditional or blanket.
